Koh Samui's kite season follows the monsoon winds. The most reliable riding is from December to April, when north-east to south-east winds blow across a shallow, reef-protected lagoon at Ban Harn and Hua Thanon on the south-east coast, one of the best beginner spots in Thailand. From May to November the wind is lighter and lessons move to Nathon on the west coast, where it blows best from about 09:00 to 12:00. April–May and October are the weakest months. A 2-hour discovery lesson costs about 3,500–4,000 THB, and most beginners need 3–5 days of lessons to ride on their own.

This is the typical pattern reported by kite schools in the Samui area, not a guarantee: a windy February week can be followed by three calm days. On good dry-season days, schools on neighbouring Koh Phangan report about 10–20 knots. Average wind at Samui airport, in the sheltered north-east corner of the island, is only about 7 knots across the year, which is why kiting concentrates on the exposed coasts in season. Check the live forecast on Windy before you plan a session.

Why the wind works like this

Samui sits in the Gulf of Thailand, between two monsoons. From about November to January the north-east monsoon brings rain and gusty north to north-east wind; as it dries out, the wind swings east and south-east and becomes the steady trade wind that makes February and March the peak kite months. From about June to September the south-west monsoon blows from the Andaman side; Samui is partly sheltered from it by the mainland, so it is lighter here than on the open sea, and best on the west coast. Between the monsoons, in May and October, the wind is light and unpredictable. The full year is explained in our weather by month guide.

Spots by wind direction

North-east to south-east wind (December–April)

Ban Harn and Hua Thanon lagoon (south-east coast). Samui's main kite spot: a shallow, sandy, reef-protected bay that stays flat in the inner lagoon, with waist-deep water ideal for learning. It works in NE, ENE, E and SE wind. Intermediate riders use the larger bays either side, and the outer reef has small waves for experienced riders. Hazards: the reef, boats and trees on the beach, and a small launch area, so launch with help. There are showers, toilets and food nearby. Ban Harn on Google Maps; see also Hua Thanon.

Chaweng and Bophut (east and north coasts). Kited on windy days, mostly by experienced riders. The problems are swimmers, boat traffic, moored longtails, chop and, at Chaweng from October to December, onshore surf and rip currents. Not for lessons.

South-west to west wind (May–November)

Nathon (west coast). The summer teaching spot, on a wide sandy beach in front of the town. The wind is lighter and best in the morning, typically 09:00–12:00. Watch for the ferry pier and boat traffic. Nathon guide.

Lipa Noi (west coast). Very shallow and calm, kited occasionally in a westerly. It's tidal: at low tide the water is too shallow to ride. Lipa Noi guide.

Tide at the lagoon

The Ban Harn lagoon is shallow, which is what makes it safe for learning, but the tide changes it through the day. Around low tide the inner lagoon can become too shallow to ride and the reef edge comes closer to the surface; around mid to high tide there is enough water to fall safely and the launch area is wider. Plan sessions for a rising or high tide when the wind allows, walk the lagoon at low tide once to see where the coral heads are, and wear booties. The tide right now: [kp_tide_now]. Our tides guide explains the pattern.

Lessons and courses

Kitesurfing is best learned in a course with radio helmets and an instructor in the water with you, on a flat, shallow spot such as the Ban Harn lagoon. A typical progression:

  1. Discovery (about 2 h) Wind theory, safety systems, flying a small trainer kite, then a real kite on the beach.
  2. Level 1–2 (about 3 days) Launching and landing, body-dragging in the water, self-rescue, first water starts.
  3. Level 3 (about 5 days in total) Riding upwind, stopping, turning and the safety knowledge to rent gear on your own.

Most beginners need 9–15 hours of lessons over 3–5 days to ride independently; people who wakeboard or snowboard often learn faster. Choose a school certified by IKO or VDWS: the certificate is recognised worldwide, so you can rent gear or continue the course elsewhere.

On Samui, Kiteboarding Asia runs lessons at the Hua Thanon lagoon from December to April and in front of its Nathon shop from May to November. Its packages combine lessons with accommodation and include an IKO licence; e-foil lessons are offered on no-wind days. Other small schools and freelance instructors work the lagoon in season; ask to see their certification before you pay.

How to choose a kite school

  • Certification: IKO or VDWS instructors, and a certificate at the end of your course.
  • Radio helmets: the instructor talks to you while you ride, which halves the shouting and speeds up learning.
  • Instructor in the water or on a rescue boat during your first water starts.
  • Flat, shallow water for beginners: the inner lagoon in season, not open chop.
  • Up-to-date gear with working safety releases, and kites sized for your weight.
  • Clear policy for no-wind days: hours carried over, not lost, or a switch to e-foil or wing foil.
  • Small groups: one instructor to one or two students on the water.

Rental and gear

Rental is for riders who can already ride upwind and self-rescue; schools will usually ask about your level, and may want to see your IKO card or watch you ride first. Supervised rental, with an instructor watching from the beach, is the step between lessons and full independence. If you bring your own gear, for an average-weight rider a mid-size kite (around 9–12 m) covers most dry-season days, with a bigger kite or a foil for the light days of April and the summer. Bring a short wetsuit top or rash vest against sun and jellyfish, booties for the reef, and a helmet. Rental shops for surf and kite equipment are concentrated around Chaweng, but on the water the lagoon on the south-east coast is where you want to be.

Wing foil, e-foil and SUP on light-wind days

Samui has many light-wind days, and some of the kite school's packages mix in wing foil, wing SUP, SUP and surfing so you are on the water every day. Wing foiling (a hand-held inflatable wing on a hydrofoil board) needs less wind than kiting and is easier to launch on a crowded beach. E-foil boards, electric hydrofoils that need no wind at all, are offered on calm days in Nathon. On flat mornings, a stand-up paddleboard is the simplest option: see kayak and SUP on Koh Samui.

Safety

  • Onshore or side-onshore only. Never ride in offshore wind, which blows you out to sea. On the west coast the north-east monsoon is offshore; on the east coast a south-west breeze is offshore.
  • Keep away from swimmers and boats. Give longtails, ferries, piers, fishing nets and swimmers a wide berth; at Nathon the ferry pier is close.
  • Squalls. In the south-west season and the monsoon changeovers, dark clouds can bring strong, sudden gusts within minutes. Land the kite as soon as you see a squall coming.
  • Reef and tide. Learn where the reef is at the lagoon and wear booties. At low tide on the west coast the water may be too shallow to fall safely.
  • Jellyfish. Box jellyfish are rare but dangerous around Samui. Wear a long-sleeved top, and know the first aid: vinegar on the sting for at least 30 seconds, no rubbing, call 1669.
  • Never kite alone and always tell someone on the beach where you are going.
  • Insurance. Check that your travel insurance covers kitesurfing; many policies need an adventure-sports add-on.

Right of way on the water

  • A rider coming in from the water has priority over one launching from the beach.
  • When two riders meet head-on, the one with the right hand forward (starboard tack) keeps their line; the other gives way.
  • The rider upwind keeps their kite high; the rider downwind keeps it low so the lines don't touch.
  • Before a jump, check you have plenty of clear water and air downwind of you.
  • Never launch or land in the middle of swimmers, and ask someone to help with a launch rather than self-launching on a crowded beach.

Reading the forecast

Look at wind speed and gusts, not just the average: a forecast of 14 knots gusting 25 is a very different day from a steady 14. Check the direction against the spot table above, and look at the hourly forecast, because sea breezes often build after midday in the dry season while the summer wind at Nathon is strongest in the morning. Windy and Open-Meteo both give hourly forecasts for Samui, and the Thai Meteorological Department posts storm warnings at tmd.go.th.

A kite week in February: a sample plan

  1. Day 1 Arrive, settle in near Hua Thanon or Lamai; walk the lagoon at low tide to see the reef and the launch.
  2. Day 2 Discovery lesson: theory, trainer kite and first flights.
  3. Day 3 Body-dragging and self-rescue in the inner lagoon.
  4. Day 4 First water starts; 2 hours on the water is plenty.
  5. Day 5 Rest or no-wind day: an e-foil or SUP session, or a boat trip from Thong Krut.
  6. Day 6 Riding short distances, stopping and turning.
  7. Day 7 Riding upwind with supervision; ask for your IKO level in your logbook.

Experienced riders can use the same week for downwind runs along the south-east coast with a friend, and a day trip to Koh Phangan's lagoons when the forecast suits.

Children and teenagers

Kitesurfing depends on weight as much as age: a light child is pulled hard by even a small kite. Most schools take children from about 10–12 years, depending on their weight and swimming, and teach them with small kites in the shallow lagoon. Under that age, a SUP or a wing-foil introduction on a calm day is a gentler start. Tell the school your child's age, weight and swimming ability when you book.

What to bring

  • Rash vest or short wetsuit top for sun and jellyfish.
  • Reef booties for the lagoon.
  • Sunglasses with a strap and a cap you can tie on.
  • Reef-safe sunscreen, applied well before you go in.
  • Your IKO card or logbook if you already ride.
  • A dry bag and plenty of water: the lagoon is exposed and hot.

Getting to the lagoon

The kite lagoon at Ban Harn is on the south-east coast just off the ring road (Route 4169), past Hua Thanon. Allow about 15 minutes from Lamai, 30–40 minutes from Chaweng and about 40 minutes from the airport, depending on traffic. Taxis and Grab cover the route; if you rent a scooter, the ring road is fine but busy, and the lane down to the beach is narrow. Find it on Google Maps, and read getting around Koh Samui for fares.

Is Samui right for your kite trip?

  • Good for: learning in flat, shallow water from December to April; couples where one partner kites and the other wants beaches, restaurants and boat trips; combining a few kite days with a family holiday.
  • Less good for: a summer kite holiday (June–September), when Koh Phangan has stronger wind; advanced freestyle riders looking for big, consistent wind every day; anyone who needs a guaranteed wind week in May or October.
  • Costs to plan for: lessons or packages, transport to the lagoon (taxis add up from Chaweng), and a few no-wind days in every fortnight.

No-wind days

Every kite trip has them. Use flat mornings for an e-foil, wing or SUP session, or take a day on the water from nearby Thong Krut: the Pig Island and Koh Tan trip runs all year and snorkels a shallow reef. Inland, the waterfalls are 20–30 minutes from Hua Thanon, and a Thai cooking class or a massage fills a rainy afternoon. Check tomorrow's wind on Windy before you book a lesson, and ask the school to move your hours to the next windy day rather than ride in marginal wind.

Kiting on Koh Phangan

Koh Phangan, 20–50 minutes away by ferry, has more kite schools and lagoons than Samui. Its Thong Sala and Ban Tai lagoons work from January to April in south-east wind, the south-west monsoon from June to September is stronger and gustier there than on Samui (often 15–25 knots), and Chaloklum on the north coast catches north-east wind in November and December. If kiting is the main point of your trip and you have a week, Phangan gives you more options; if you're staying on Samui from December to April, the Ban Harn lagoon is as good a place to learn as any in the Gulf. See kitesurfing on Koh Phangan on our sister site, and Koh Samui to Koh Phangan for the ferries.

Where to stay and what else to do

For the December–April season, stay on the south coast around Hua Thanon, Ban Harn or Laem Set to be minutes from the lagoon, or in Lamai, about 15–20 minutes away. From May to November, stay in Nathon or on the west coast near Lipa Noi. Non-kiting partners are close to plenty: Pig Island boats leave from nearby Thong Krut on the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB, all year), and Lamai's beach and restaurants are a short drive.
